newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Southeast Asian currency war hurts speculators.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian currency war hurts speculators.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit and Indonesian rupiah jumped in early trade on Friday as speculators found themselves cut off from short-term funds needed to cover their positions, dealers said.

They said Bank Negara, Malaysia's central bank, appeared to have asked local banks to stop lending money for up to two days to foreign borrowers, as the Thai central bank did on Thursday in an effort to squeeze out speculators.
Bank Negara said its current monetary policy stance remained unchanged.
Analysts said the market was surprised by the way the region's central banks had been able to cut liquidity to the offshore markets without affecting domestic interbank interest rates.

They said this had been achieved by persuading domestic banks not to lend money to offshore players who had gone short in the currency -- sold currency they did not have in expectation of being able to finalise the deal with money bought later at a lower rate.
Usually they borrow on a short term basis -- technically called tommorow/next, meaning they have to pay it back with interest in a couple of days.
A U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said such loans were carrying something "like a 500 percent (annual) interest rate", making them just too expensive for speculators.
Dealers said overseas funds were being forced to sell dollars in the spot market to cover their short positions in the ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah.

"A lot of funds are cutting their long dollar positions. It's a bloodbath. The funds have been hurt very badly," the dealer said of those who had to pay hugely expensive interest rates for currency to close their positions.
The ringgit rose to a high of 2.4750 against the dollar in early trade against its opening around 2.4900. It was quoted at 2.4910/20 at 0335 GMT.
In Jakarta, market talk that Malaysian authorities planned to scrap swap facilities caused offshore players to flood the Indonesian swap market, pushing the rupiah to a high of 2,413.0.
Bank Negara specifically denied this.

"There are a lot of rumours in the market. We don't know what is true. But people are saying swap facilities could be scrapped in Malaysia, triggering a slew of switches to Indonesia," a Jakarta dealer said before Bank Negara spoke.
By 0335 GMT, the rupiah had slipped back to 2,434.0/36.0 but was still well above its opening 2,440.0/45.0.
The Thai baht remained relatively firm but off its highs, at around the 25.450/25.650 to the dollar at 0335 GMT against a high of 25.300/25.340 late on Thursday.

Singapore dealers said the tom/next rate had also settled down after rising to a peak of 200 satangs on Thursday, but rumours that Thai banks were still not being allowed to quote tom/next to offshore players persisted.
"There seems to be a concerted move by central banks to squeeze out the speculators," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.

"Generally the speculative, especially the U.S. hedge funds and short-term European funds, are learning a lesson, which is not a bad thing. But in the short term, it could have a negative impact on foreign direct investment," he added.
Dealers said money market liquidity in Singapore had also tightened in what appeared to be a spillover effect from the volatility in other centres.
The release of Singapore's first quarter gross domestic product and other economic indicators was largely eclipsed by the activity in the ringgit and rupiah, dealers said.
The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4321/31 at 0335 GMT.

Dealers said Bank Negara Malaysia appeared to have asked local banks to stop lending money to foreign borrowers for up to two days at a time, as the Thai central bank did on Thursday in a move to squeeze speculators out of the market.

The talk triggered fears the Indonesian authorities would follow suit, pushing the ringgit and rupiah to lows of 2.4735 and 2,413.00 respectively against the dollar, as players sold their dollar holdings in the spot market to obtain funds.
The Malaysian and Indonesian central banks denied they had told banks to stop swap transactions, bringing some semblance of calm back to the market, dealers said.
Market participants are usually able to borrow on a short term basis -- technically called tomorrow/next, meaning they have to pay it back with interest in a couple of days.
This allows them to go short in a currency, or sell a currency they do not have in anticiapation of it falling and being able to finalise the deal with money bought later at a lower rate.
A U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said the early surge in tomorrow/next rates for the ringgit and rupiah had made the cost of holding such loans much too expensive for speculators.

"Dealers said it was not clear whether the central bank had indeed asked Kuala Lumpur banks to stop quoting tom/next rates to offshore parties, as the Thai central bank did on Thursday to squeeze out speculators.

But they said local banks had definitely been reluctant to quote to offshore players, pushing tom/next rates up sharply and causing funds to sell dollars on the spot market to cover their short ringgit positions.

"If you're a local bank and you see swaps are so tight, and if you're very long, you just sit back and relax and people will take you regardless of the spread," said a European bank dealer in Singapore.

In the Philippines, the peso firmed against the dollar after the central bank again sold dollars and raised overnight interest rates by seven percentage points to 20 percent, their highest level since March 1995.
The head of trading at a European bank in Singapore gave a theoretical example of just how much money had been won and lost during the events of the last few days.

"If you took a US$10 (million) long position in six month baht forwards on Tuesday, you'd have been down around $80,000 by Wednesday. I suppose that's manageable and you could decide to run (keep) it," he said.
"But on Thursday the rates moved so suddenly, so violently, you're losing a fortune. Right now that position would mean a loss of $440,000," he said.

Sim Moh Siong, regional economist at Citibank in Singapore, said the supply of funds had essentially dried up in regional currency markets due to fears of a possible spillover from Thursday's liquidity squeeze in the Thai baht.

Speculators who had gone short on the baht aggressively this week amid concerns of a slowing Thai economy and talk of political turmoil in the cabinet were badly burned by the Thai central bank's moves to support its currency.

"What was done was to isolate the offshore money market from the onshore market such that those who had sold the currency before would now suffer losses because of lack of funding," Sim told Reuters Financial Television.
Analysts said the market was surprised by the way the region's central banks had cut liquidity to the offshore markets without affecting domestic interbank interest rates.
Regional central banks appeared to have emerged on top in the battle against speculators. The Bank of Thailand declared victory in its defence of the baht.
But economists said the central banks could ultimately pay a high price for their win.

"Investors are now likely to demand a higher interest differential to offset the increased risk of holding these currencies and this could hurt the economy, especially if it's suffering a slowdown," Citibank's Sim said.
Daniel Lian, Asian Bond and Currency Strategist at NatWest Markets, said there were likely to be more speculative attacks.
"The next round the speculators will be better prepared for coordinated actions by both the BOT and regional central banks," Lian said in a market commentary.
